Expected Utility vs Expected Profit

In micro, one person's attitude to risk and one firm's choice were studied apart. In macro, those attitudes add up and move the whole economy.

People dislike shaky outcomes, so they buy insurance. Given the same average, they pick the sure thing. Firms read only average profit and take the riskier project. Splitting it among many shareholders shrinks the shakiness. The formulas below set the two yardsticks side by side. Everything here is risk, where the odds are known.

For example, say a coin flip decides your 💰 allowance. Heads pays 10,000 won, tails pays nothing. The average is 5,000 won, yet you might prefer a sure 4,500. The 500 you give up out of caution is just like an insurance premium.

Examples & Exercises

One coin flip makes your wealth 160160160 or 404040 (fifty-fifty).

For a person with utility u(x)=xu(x) = \sqrt{x}u(x)=x​, what is the gamble's certainty equivalent, and what is the risk premium?

Show proof

  1. Expected wealth is E[W]=0.5⋅160+0.5⋅40=100E[W] = 0.5 \cdot 160 + 0.5 \cdot 40 = 100E[W]=0.5⋅160+0.5⋅40=100. Expected utility averages the utility, not the money: EU=0.5160+0.540≈9.49EU = 0.5\sqrt{160} + 0.5\sqrt{40} \approx 9.49EU=0.5160​+0.540​≈9.49.

  2. The certainty equivalent is CE=EU2CE = EU^2CE=EU2, and the square comes out exact: 14(160+40+2160⋅40)=14(200+160)=90\frac{1}{4}(160 + 40 + 2\sqrt{160 \cdot 40}) = \frac{1}{4}(200 + 160) = 9041​(160+40+2160⋅40​)=41​(200+160)=90. The risk premium is 100−90=10100 - 90 = 10100−90=10 — a sure 909090 feels exactly as good as this gamble averaging 100100100.

  3. Read as insurance: a loss of 120120120 hits with probability 0.50.50.5, so the fair premium is 0.5⋅120=600.5 \cdot 120 = 600.5⋅120=60, and full insurance locks in wealth 100100100 — better than CE=90CE = 90CE=90. The most this person pays in total is 160−90=70160 - 90 = 70160−90=70, exactly the risk premium 101010 above the fair premium.

A firm must choose between a safe project (profit 404040 for sure) and a risky one (profit 808080 or 202020, fifty-fifty).

If a shareholder instead holds 161616 independent copies of the risky project, what is the spread of the average profit, and the chance the average falls below the safe profit 404040?

Show proof

  1. The firm looks only at expected profit: the risky project gives 0.5⋅80+0.5⋅20=50>400.5 \cdot 80 + 0.5 \cdot 20 = 50 > 400.5⋅80+0.5⋅20=50>40, so it takes the risky one — even though it can come out at 202020. The yardstick is the average of profit, not of utility.

  2. One project's spread is σ=30\sigma = 30σ=30.

    The average of NNN independent copies has spread σ/N\sigma / \sqrt{N}σ/N​, so with 161616 copies it shrinks to 30/4=7.530 / 4 = 7.530/4=7.5.

    The average falls below 404040 only when at most 555 of the 161616 come out high — probability about 10.5%10.5\%10.5% (with a single copy it is 50%50\%50%).

  3. So the shareholder barely feels the risk: the expected profit 505050 survives while the danger evaporates. That is why a household tied to one undiversifiable job and a diversified shareholder face the same gamble with opposite attitudes.
